chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who borrows a loan from another man and gives him collateral, whether a servant, or utensils, or clothes, and he needs something from its benefit, so he asks permission for it and he grants permission. He said: 'If his soul is pleased, there is no harm.' I said: 'Indeed, those among us narrate that every loan that brings benefit is invalid.' He said: 'Is not the best loan that which brings benefit?'
ai.seo_question: Is a loan valid if the borrower benefits from the collateral item?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Shia juristic distinction between *riba al-jahiliyya* (excessive interest) and permissible benefit (*manfa'a*) derived from collateral. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) resolves the apparent contradiction with other narrations by emphasizing the lender's consent (*riḍā*), thereby validating loans where the borrower uses the pledged item with permission. This underscores the flexibility in Shia commercial law, prioritizing mutual agreement over rigid prohibitions on any form of benefit.
